27.0.0.en: 1 Moreover Job continued his parable, and said, 2 "As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment; and the Almighty, who hath vexed my soul; 3 All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils; 4 My lips shall not speak wickedness, nor my tongue utter deceit. 5 God forbid that I should justify you: till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me. 6 My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go: my heart shall not reproach any of my days.

27.0.1.en: Moreover Job continued his parable, and said: [1]

27.1.0.en: As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment; and the Almighty, who hath vexed my soul [2]

27.1.1.en: Some think that the word "parable" is the one used as the title of the Book of the Proverbs of Solomon, because it is full of teachings. Now Job speaks as in parables, with authority, like one who has triumphed over his adversaries. He speaks like one who is bringing the dialogue to a close, giving an oath: "As God liveth," for [an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife] (Heb 6:16). Job swears to establish his integrity and uprightness, and declares his innocence of the accusations brought against him.

27.1.2.en: He swears by the living God, as the only Judge possessing absolute authority, who knows the depths of the heart and the inner thoughts, so that His judgment is true and right.

27.1.3.en: "Who hath taken away my judgment," that is, who has refused to do him justice in the discussion, to show his innocence and to defend him; Elihu had already rebuked him for this (Job 34:5); for God is just in all His ways, and it is not possible that He should take away any man's right.

27.1.4.en: "And the Almighty, who hath vexed my soul"; without doubt Job knew that the Almighty God is also the loving, tender and wise One. For with His power there is in Him a compassionate fatherhood, and in wisdom He chooses the fitting time to vindicate His believers and to offer them consolations, but in a moment of weakness he uttered this. This accusation comes from man because of his inability to wait for the right time for God's defense of him and support of him. It is not He who makes our souls bitter, but our impatience and our inability to perceive God's love and wisdom that cause us this bitterness.

27.1.5.en: If the enemy of good never ceases to seek to tempt men unjustly and carelessly, because with his evil will he desires their destruction, God with His good will allows men to be tempted, out of His concern for them, to prove them, or to justify them, or to purify them and for their spiritual growth and their enjoyment of glory. Therefore, even if Satan spares no effort to tempt the believer, the believer who is confident of God's care for him counts that he is tempted by divine permission for his edification.

27.1.6.en: * "As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment; and the Almighty, who hath brought my soul to bitterness" [2]. By these very words Job tells us of his circumstances, and gives us a picture of the Church under affliction, surrounded by the boldness of unbelievers and tossed about by the bitterness of persecutors. The Church is tempted by her adversaries in two ways: she is persecuted either by words or by swords. Now the Holy Church, by her great striving, aims at acquiring wisdom and patience. She exercises wisdom when she is tempted by words, and exercises patience when she is tempted by swords.

27.1.7.en: In any case, he speaks now of that persecution which is raised not by swords but by vain words. We know that some, when faced with an unseemly matter, deny the existence of God, and some believe in the existence of God but reckon that He does not care about the affairs of men.

27.1.8.en: Of the former David said: [The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God] (Ps 1:14). And of the latter he says: [How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?](a) And also: [They say, The LORD shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it] (Ps 7:94).

27.1.9.en: Thus this person, who bore the figure of the Holy Church, answered both parties in the midst of the bitterness of his grief. For as life has existence and death has none, he proclaims that God exists, saying: "As God liveth," and so he also tells that God cares for the affairs of those who are subject to death, and adds: [Who hath taken away my judgment, and brought my soul to bitterness]. For he testifies that the evils he suffers did not happen by chance, but by God who orders all things, and Job does not ascribe the force of his bitterness to the one who tempts him but to his Creator...

27.1.10.en: The will of Satan is evil, but since God permits it, its power is just. For on his part (Satan) seeks to tempt men unjustly and without concern, but as for those who are sought to be tempted, when they are so sought, God does not allow them to be tempted except justly.

27.1.12.en: * We ought to know that all men are tempted for three reasons:

27.1.15.en: (c) And in some cases because of their sins. 1- For their proving, as we read of the blessed Abraham and Job and many saints who endured countless trials. 2- And for correction, when He chastens His righteous ones for their slight (involuntary) sins and lapses, and so as to raise them to a greater state of purity, cleansing them from defiled thoughts, as in the saying: "Many are the afflictions of the righteous" (Ps 19:34), [My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. For what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons] (Heb 5:12-8). And in the Book of Revelation: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Rev 19:3). And David prays for this gift of cleansing, saying: "Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart" (Ps 2:26). And since the prophet knows the value of these trials, he says: "O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger" (Jer 24:10), and also "O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me" (Isa 1:12). 3- As a punishment for sin, just as God threatened to send plagues upon the children of Israel because of their wickedness: "I will also send the teeth of beasts upon them, with the poison of serpents of the dust" (Deut 24:32). And also in the Psalms: "Many sorrows shall be to the wicked" (Ps 10:32), and in the Gospel it is written: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (Jn 14:5). 4- In truth we find also a fourth cause mentioned by Holy Scripture, which is that troubles are brought upon us simply to manifest the glory of God and His works, as the Gospel says: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him" (Jn 3:9). And also: "This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby" (Jn 4:11). 5- And there are other kinds of vengeances with which are afflicted those who have exceeded the bonds of evil in their lives (and carried it to excess), for we read of Dathan and Abiram and Korah, who were punished, and of those of whom the Apostle says: "God gave them up unto vile affections... unto a reprobate mind" (Rom 1:26, 28). These are counted the most bitter of all punishments, because they have become unworthy to be healed by the life-giving divine visitation, for "being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness" (Eph 4:19). And because of the hardness of their hearts and their persistence in their habits and their doing of evil, there has come upon them a punishment in this world without cleansing. And the Holy Word reproaches them, which the prophet spoke, saying: "I have overthrown some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD" (Amos 11:4). And Jeremiah says: "I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways" (Jer 7:15). And also "Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction: they have made their faces harder than a rock; they have refused to return" (Jer 3:5). The prophet sees that all the remedies of this life have brought no benefit for their healing, declaring that he has despaired of their life, saying: "The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away. Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the LORD hath rejected them" (Jer 29:6, 30).

27.1.16.en: God laments over them because He offered them cleansing by fire and they did not benefit, being hardened in their sins. So He weeps over them in the person of Jerusalem, which was coated with rust, saying: "Then set it empty upon the coals thereof, that the brass of it may be hot, and may burn, and that the filthiness of it may be molten in it, that the scum of it may be consumed. She hath wearied herself with lies, and her great scum went not forth out of her: her scum shall be in the fire. In thy filthiness is lewdness: because I have purged thee, and thou wast not purged, thou shalt not be purged from thy filthiness any more" (Ezek 11:24-13).

27.1.17.en: He is like the skilful physician who has used all means of healing and for whom there is no treatment left that can be used... Therefore God says: "So will I make my fury toward thee to rest, and my jealousy shall depart from thee, and I will be quiet, and will be no more angry" (Ezek 42:16).

27.1.18.en: Father Theodore * When God wishes to give a man victory and to exalt him, He first delivers him to evil (trials), to be tested and examined, and then He shows his beauty to the world by the good things that God does with him.

27.1.19.en: When God wished to give Joseph victory and make him lord over Egypt, as your holiness sees, what was the beginning of His work, that it might lead to a good end? First his brothers seized him, and insulted him, and mocked him, and stripped off his garments, and left him in the pit, and cut off his hope, and sold him to merchants, and he became a slave serving masters, and the handsome son of free men, who had done no wrong, was enslaved.

27.1.20.en: Whoever saw this evil deed could not have supposed that all these evils were being committed for Joseph's good. But God, who knew what He wished to do for him, did not spare him when he was crushed under the weight of all these evils, but let him fall into the pit, and be sold to merchants, and be thrown into prison unjustly. After all these things his beauty shone forth like the sun, and his right was displayed like gold, and his evils vanished like smoke, and he mounted the height of the chariot like a king, and rose to the greatness for which God had set him, so that he humbled himself and was exalted.

27.2.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils [3]

27.2.1.en: In the name of every believer earnest in his spiritual life, Job declares a sincere resolve for the holy life and the rejection of every sin. As long as there is a breath of life, we shall not utter an unseemly word. Job knew that his life was swift breaths, or moments, so that he must remain faithful to the last breath.

27.2.2.en: On the other hand, Job knows that the breaths of his life are a gift from God, who breathed into Adam his father the breath of life; it is God who gives to all life and breath and all things (Job 10:12)(*), so it is fitting for us to glorify Him in everything as long as there is a breath of life in us.

27.2.3.en: St. Ambrose comments on Job's expression "the spirit of God is in my nostrils," saying that he does not mean the bodily nostrils, but the nostrils of the inner man, which breathes in the fragrance of eternal life.

27.2.4.en: * Certainly he does not mean here by his spirit (the breath of God) the living breath and the passing bodily breath, but the nostrils of the inner man, in which the sweet fragrance of eternal life is smelled, and the dew of the grace of the heavenly anointing, as a sense of a double kind.

27.2.5.en: St. Ambrose The Holy Spirit of God, who renews our inner man, draws our whole being to enjoy the heavenly God, so that we rejoice in His heavenly divine fragrance. God breathes in His beloved children a fragrance of satisfaction and delight (Gen 8:21), as happened after the Flood when Noah offered a sacrifice to God, and the Lord Christ speaks to His bride: "The smell of thy nose like apples" (Song 7:8); and so we also breathe in our Christ the fragrance of eternal life.

27.2.6.en: * The Spirit of God cannot dwell in anyone who walks according to the things of the flesh.

27.3.0.en: Father Ambrosiaster My lips shall not speak wickedness, nor my tongue utter deceit [4].

27.3.1.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) has a wonderful comment on this phrase, saying that Job did not say, "I will not think wickedness," but "My lips shall not speak wickedness," because uttering wickedness is lighter than thinking it, for words often slip from our mouths without our will, but as for our thoughts, they are often the subject of evil and wicked preoccupation. Job resolved that his lips would not utter a wicked word, nor his tongue speak a lie, for he speaks the truth, even if it contains a condemnation of himself. He does not cover up any sin in his life with a word of deceit; in other words, hypocrisy has no place in his life or in his words.

27.3.2.en: * There is a vast difference between the expression "speak" and the expression "meditate or think." Sometimes vain thinking is worse than uttering it. For often when a person speaks the error occurs inadvertently, but thinking carries premeditated evil!

27.3.4.en: God forbid that I should justify you!

27.4.0.en: Till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me [5].

27.4.1.en: Likewise, in frankness, Job was not ready to flatter his friends with a word of deceit in order to win them at the cost of the purity of his heart, for he speaks nothing but what he carries within him. As the Apostle Paul says: "For we trust we have a good conscience, in all things willing to live honestly" (Heb 13:18). The prophet Ezekiel attacked the false prophets because, for material or social gain, they flattered the wicked, saying: "Peace; and there was no peace" (Ezek 13:10), or as the prophet Isaiah says of them that they "speak unto us smooth things" (Isa 30:10).

27.4.2.en: * It was not possible for Job to flatter his companions and justify their errors, for he had set his death before his eyes, and did not wish to depart from this world having lost his innocence, whatever the cost.

27.4.3.en: He would lose his innocence if he counted the wicked righteous, as Solomon testifies, saying: [He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD] (Prov 15:17). For there are persons who glorify the evil deeds of men; they glorify what they ought to rebuke. Thus it was said by the prophet: [Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes (the elbow of the hand), and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature] (cf. Ezek 18:13), for the pillow is placed there so that we may rest more easily. So whoever flatters persons who practice wrong places pillows under the head or elbow of one who lies asleep!

27.4.5.en: Job preferred to die holding to his integrity rather than flatter the wicked, for "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!" (Isa 5:20).

27.4.6.en: My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go.

27.5.0.en: My heart shall not reproach any of my days [6].

27.5.1.en: Job assures them that their bitter criticisms of him will not shake his depths, for he knows the love of God that is in his heart, and his strong resolve to practice goodness, and that no one will be able to take from him his inner joy in this life. If they reproach him unjustly, he will not allow his heart to reproach him. What concerns him is not men's criticisms of him, but the purity of his heart. When the prophet David sinned, his heart smote him, "And David said unto the LORD, I have sinned greatly in that I have done: and now, I beseech thee, O LORD, take away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly" (2 Sam 24:10). What accuses us is our heart, in which the Holy Spirit of God works, convicting us of sin.

27.5.2.en: * "I will not forsake my righteousness which I have begun to hold fast" [6]. For if anyone praises persons who commit sin, he forsakes the righteousness with which he began....

27.5.3.en: "For my heart shall not reproach me in all my life" [6]. It is as though he expresses himself in plain words: Take into account that I must not withdraw into iniquity, just as I fear to commit sin in my affairs... Perhaps someone will ask: On what ground does he declare that his heart does not reproach him, when he accused himself before of having sinned, saying: [I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men?] (Job 20:7). Or affirms: [If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me] (Job 20:9). We must know that there are sins which the righteous can avoid, and there are some sins which even the righteous cannot avoid. What heart of a man bound to the corruptible body does not slip into a thought that inclines toward evil, even if it does not rush into the pit of consenting to it? And yet to think this sinful thought is to commit sin. But if there is resistance to the thought, the soul is freed from confusion. So the gold of the righteous man, though freed from evil practice, sometimes falls into an evil thought...

27.5.5.en: * Although the servants and friends of God avoid the sins that lead to death, and practice many good works, we do not believe that they are without trivial sins, for God does not lie when He says: "None is pure from pollution, though his life be but one day upon the earth" (Job 4:14-5) LXX.. Add to this the blessed John the Evangelist, who is without doubt no less than James in his worthiness, and who declares: [If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us] (1 Jn 8:1). Moreover, we read in another place: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 16:24).

27.6.s.en: 2. His dread of the charge of hypocrisy

27.6.0.en: 7 "Let mine enemy be as the wicked, and he that riseth up against me as the unrighteous. 8 For what is the hope of the ungodly, though he hath gained, when God taketh away his soul? 9 Will God hear his cry when trouble cometh upon him? 10 Will he delight himself in the Almighty? will he always call upon God?"

27.6.1.en: Let mine enemy be as the wicked, and he that riseth up against me as the unrighteous [7].

27.6.2.en: Since Job was in a state of bewilderment at his friends' accusation that he was wicked and deserved harsher chastisements than had befallen him, and that he must expect total destruction, he assured them that he was not the wicked man they imagined. Now he tells them that he is far from accepting any evil way or finding pleasure in it, for if he had a most bitter enemy he would wish him to be wicked, since nothing is worse than this. This does not mean that he hates persons as his enemies and desires them to be so, but is a way of showing how much he hates evil, as the prophet Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar: "The dream be to them that hate thee" (Dan 4:19).

27.6.3.en: It is as though Job were saying that he would wish to be in any condition, such as becoming poor, or a despised slave, or bereft of his children, and not be wicked, for "sin... might become exceeding sinful" (Rom 7:13). And as the Lord Christ says: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" (Jn 8:34). And the Apostle John says: "Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law" (1 Jn 3:4); "He that committeth sin is of the devil; for the devil sinneth from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil" (1 Jn 3:8).

27.6.4.en: * "Let mine enemy be as the wicked." Sometimes the word "as" comes not for comparison but to depict a reality. For example: "We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father" (Jn 14:1). Here the word "as" comes for emphasis and not for comparison.

27.6.6.en: * Sins harm the soul with a greater gravity than worms harm the body. And yet we do not perceive their corruption, nor do we feel the pressing need to be cleansed of them. It is like the drunkard, who cannot recognize how repulsive the taste of wine is, whereas the sober man can easily discern it. So it is with sins: he who lives with dignity easily discerns the mire and corruption, but he who lives in evil is like one drunk with strong drink, and does not realize that he is sick. This is the worst thing about sin, that it does not allow those who have fallen into it to perceive the state of grave sickness they are in, but they are like those who lie in mire and think they are enjoying perfumes. They have not the least desire to be freed. And while the worm works in them they boast like those who have precious stones. Therefore they do not wish to kill it, but to revive it and multiply it until it carries them across to the worm in the life to come.

27.7.0.en: St. John Chrysostom For what is the hope of the ungodly, when he cuts off, when God taketh away his soul? [8]

27.7.1.en: Some translate this phrase, "For what is the hope of the hypocrite, though he hath gained any profit, when God taketh away his spirit?" The wicked man, especially the hypocrite, lives without hope, for his end is eternal destruction. Since his friends accused him of hypocrisy, he assures them that he is not so foolish as to practice hypocrisy with his hope shattered. For if hypocrisy offers temporal gain, which is men's praise of him or the obtaining of temporal wealth, this is only a temporary deception, which appears when the hypocrite's soul is required of him, and all that is in his heart is exposed. The psalmist says of the hypocrite: "For when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him" (Ps 49:17). As the Scripture says: "Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and take heed what thou speakest" (Sir 1:37).

27.7.2.en: * "For what is the hope of the hypocrite, if greed hold him fast, and God free not his soul?" [8] The hypocrite, who in Latin is called simulator, that is, a pretender, has no aim but to appear.

27.7.4.en: * God hates hypocrisy, and man abhors it. It brings no reward, and is wholly without benefit for the salvation of the soul, but rather is a cause of its destruction.

27.7.5.en: If hypocrisy is sometimes not exposed, it is only for a time, for it does not last long, but everything is revealed, and brings calamity on its owner, and so it is like an ugly-looking woman from whom her outward adornment, put on her by artificial means, is stripped off.

27.7.6.en: * Hypocrisy is foreign to the character of the saints, for it is impossible that anything we do or say should escape the eyes of the Godhead, since "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known." All our words and deeds will be revealed on the day of judgment. Therefore hypocrisy is wearisome and without benefit. It is fitting for us to prove ourselves true worshippers, serving God with open and clear countenance.

27.8.0.en: St. Cyril the Great Will God hear his cry when trouble cometh upon him? [9]

27.8.1.en: The prayer of the hypocrite is not answered; distress will come upon him and he will cry out, but his cry is worthless. God does not hear the cries of hypocrites until they leave their hypocrisy, and offer repentance, and return to Him. The Lord says to the prophet Isaiah: "Fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites" (Isa 33:14). "If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me" (Ps 66:18). "He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination" (Prov 28:9). The wicked will cry out on the day of the Lord and God will not hear them. The Lord says: "Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded; but ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof: I also will laugh at your calamity" (Prov 1:24-26).

27.8.2.en: Poor is the hypocrite, for he will not experience the peace of God and His consolations, and does not delight in the Almighty, because his delight is in the riches of the world, and its passing glory, and in the pleasures and lusts of the flesh. The hypocrite does not know how to call upon God, for in time of prosperity he amuses himself with what he has and makes light of spiritual worship, and in time of distress he murmurs and blasphemes against God.

27.8.3.en: The hypocrite does not know how to call upon Him, because God has no place in his heart, for God does not dwell with hypocrisy, nor truth with deceit and guile.

27.8.4.en: The hypocrite may believe in the existence of God, and that He is Almighty and that one must pray to Him, but in practice there is no place for God in his depths. He thinks that his real power lies in what he gains of temporal things, and his reliance is on his possessions, his authority and his friendships, not on God the Almighty!

27.8.5.en: The aim of the Church is to present the Lord Christ to the world, that He may tell all about the Father, and declare His mighty plan for the salvation of mankind.

27.8.6.en: As the Church experiences fellowship with her Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus, who is called the hand of God, she tastes the sweetness of the mysteries of God, and experiences His strength and power, and so calls all to share with her in this joyful experience.

27.8.7.en: * "Will God hear his cry when trouble cometh upon him? Or will he be able to delight himself in the Almighty?" [9] God does not hear his cry in time of distress, because in time of quiet he did not listen to the Lord who cries out in His commandments. It is written: [He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination] (Prov 9:28). Since the holy man sees that all who now care nothing for practicing what is upright will in the end be terrified at the words of entreaty... Thus the prophet says: [Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near] (Isa 6:55).

27.8.8.en: Now God is not seen, and He is near; afterward He will be seen and will not be near. He has not yet appeared in judgment, so if He is sought He is found. For when He appears in judgment in a wonderful way, He is seen and is not found.

27.8.9.en: Thus Solomon describes Wisdom as embracing with sweetness and judging with awe, saying: "Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets."

27.8.11.en: The Lord Christ urges us to secret prayer, to keep us from the hypocrisy that spoils prayer so that it is not answered.

27.8.12.en: * In the same way our Savior taught us this kind of prayer. You must pray in secret to Him who is in secret and sees all, as the Lord Christ said: "Enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly" (Mt 6:6).

27.8.13.en: My beloved, why does our Savior teach us, saying: [Pray to your Father in secret, with the door shut]?

27.8.14.en: I will show you this as far as I am able.

27.8.15.en: The words of our Lord make known to us that you must pray with your heart in secret, with the door shut, but what is the door that you must shut? Is it not your mouth, because it is the temple in which Christ dwells, as the Apostle said: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God?" (1 Cor 3:16), so that God may enter into your inner man in this dwelling, which must be cleansed of everything unclean, while the door, that is, your mouth, is shut.

27.8.16.en: St. Aphrahat * God Himself is invisible, so He wishes your prayer also to be invisible.

27.8.17.en: St. John Chrysostom * Above all we must observe with all care the Gospel commandment that bids us enter into our closet and shut our door and pray to our Father. And this is accomplished as follows:

27.8.18.en: * We pray within our closet when we remove from our inner hearts disturbing thoughts and vain cares, and enter into a secret, closed conversation between ourselves and the Lord.

27.8.19.en: * We pray with doors shut when we pray with closed lips, in perfect quiet and silence, to Him who seeks hearts and not words.

27.8.20.en: * We pray in secret when we keep hidden our petitions that come from our hearts and our burning minds, so that we reveal them to God alone, and the opposing powers (the demons) cannot discover them. Therefore we must pray in complete silence, not only to avoid disturbing our brethren near us and troubling them with our whispering or loud words, and to avoid upsetting the thoughts of those who pray with us, but in order to hide the meaning of our petitions from our enemies who watch us, especially at the time of prayer, and thus is fulfilled the commandment: "Keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom" (Mic 5:7).

27.8.21.en: Father Isaac Will he delight himself in the Almighty?

27.9.0.en: Will he always call upon God? [10]

27.9.1.en: Some think that he means here: What hope has the wicked man or the hypocrite, even if he gains much wealth according to the desire of his heart? Will his cry be heard at once when he is in distress? And others think that Job knows that there is no profit for the wicked man even if he gains much, for he will surely depart, and will be a terror to the hypocrite.

27.10.s.en: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

27.10.0.en: 11 "I will teach you by the hand of God: that which is with the Almighty will I not conceal. 12 Behold, all ye yourselves have seen it; why then are ye thus altogether vain? saying, 13 This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage of oppressors, which they shall receive of the Almighty. 14 If his children be multiplied, it is for the sword: and his offspring shall not be satisfied with bread. 15 Those that remain of him shall be buried in death: and his widows shall not weep. 16 Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare raiment as the clay; 17 He may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver. 18 He buildeth his house as a moth, and as a booth that the keeper maketh. 19 The rich man shall lie down, but he shall not be gathered: he openeth his eyes, and he is not. 20 Terrors take hold on him as waters, a tempest stealeth him away in the night. 21 The east wind carrieth him away, and he departeth: and as a storm hurleth him out of his place. 22 For God shall cast upon him, and not spare: he would fain flee out of his hand. 23 Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place."

27.10.1.en: I will teach you by the hand of God.

27.10.2.en: That which is with the Almighty will I not conceal [11].

27.10.3.en: Job affirms that his knowledge of the divine mysteries he has received as from the hand of God, and that he does not hold back from declaring what he has received. In this he is a type of the Church, which was taught the truth by the Lord Christ, who is the Truth Himself, who came to tell us about the Father.

27.10.4.en: Since Job is a type of the persecuted Church, in her name he declares her mission, which is to teach men by the hand of God, that is, by Christ Jesus, for the hand of God signifies the Son the Word, and the finger of God signifies the Holy Spirit.

27.10.5.en: St. Clement of Alexandria often called the Lord Christ the Teacher, or Trainer, or Instructor, Paedagogus. The saint distinguished between the divine Logos as guide, Protrepikos, as tutor, Paedagogus, and as teacher, Didaskelos. As the Guide He calls men to salvation; as the Tutor He urges believers to the better life and heals them of their passions, exercising His spiritual work in them; and finally He is Himself the Teacher, Didaskalos, who teaches the general foundations and explains them, interpreting the symbolic sayings.

27.10.6.en: And from the saint's own words: [The heavenly Guide, the Logos, is called the Guide when He calls mankind to salvation... but as He works as a physician or tutor His name becomes "the Tutor"... For the sick soul needs a tutor who heals its passions. Then it needs the teacher who gives it understanding... "the revelation of the Logos." Thus, since the Logos desires our salvation step by step, He uses an excellent method. At the beginning He guides, then He corrects, and finally He teaches.]

27.10.7.en: * There is no knowledge without faith, and no faith without knowledge... The Son is the true Teacher about the Father. We believe in the Son in order to know the Father, with whom also is the Son. Again, in order to know the Father we must believe in the Son, the Son of the Father.

27.10.8.en: The knowledge of the Father and the Son, in the manner of the true Gnostic, is the attainment of the truth by means of the truth... Truly, few are those who believe and know.

27.10.9.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * The blessed Job speaks in a way, pointing to a matter that concerns us. For the Holy Church in her teaching explains the truth that we may know it, and does not hide the least part of the truth. Thus because "the hand of God" is a name of the Son, since by Him all things were made (Jn 3:1), she affirms that by the hand of God she teaches those whom she sees continuing in ignorance by clinging to their own wisdom. It is as if she says plainly: [I know nothing of myself, but what I perceive of the truth I understand by the generosity of the Truth].

27.11.0.en: Behold, all ye yourselves have seen it; why then are ye thus altogether vain? saying, [12]

27.11.1.en: Here he rebukes those who have knowledge and do not teach, for this is sin, as the Apostle says (Jas 17:4).

27.11.2.en: What did they see in Job? Truly his soul was greatly embittered by their false accusations, which added to his afflictions a still harsher affliction. But with all this he did not blaspheme against God, nor ascribe injustice to Him. In the bitterness of his soul he asked to stand before God to be judged, for he is certain that He is just and loving and will acquit him.

27.11.3.en: In reproach he says to them: Why do you speak falsehood? Why do you hunt for faults in me? Why do you not judge me by the reality in which I live? Why did you not perceive what lies behind my words, a living faith in the Almighty God?

27.12.0.en: This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage of oppressors, which they shall receive of the Almighty [13].

27.12.1.en: He says to them: Why do you speak falsehood against me? If I suffer misfortunes and blows, look at what is the portion of the wicked man in this world, and the heritage of oppressors here? For many of them are successful, and men of authority, and rich... but only for a moment, and everything they have collapses, if not in this world then in the life to come. Behold, practical reality testifies that not all the righteous are at ease, nor all the wicked in distress! Do not be hasty in judging me!

27.13.0.en: If his children be multiplied, it is for the sword: and his offspring shall not be satisfied with bread [14].

27.13.1.en: The offspring of the wicked man suffer hunger, for they do not find the bread necessary to be satisfied. And if there is food, they eat, and there is no satisfaction (cf. Hag 1:6). It may also mean their need to taste the heavenly bread, the word of God that satisfies the soul, in that a famine for the word comes upon them. "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD" (Amos 8:11).

27.14.0.en: Those that remain of him shall be buried in death (in plague): and his widows shall not weep [15].

27.14.1.en: His offspring become a burden on society, so that even in their death no one honors them, and as it was said in Jeremiah: [He shall be buried with the burial of an ass] (Jer 22:19). When they die their widows do not weep for them, for there is no reason to grieve over them, since the widows are relieved of them, and count their death a rest for themselves.

27.14.2.en: * Job describes the wretched portion of the wicked. For though they have many children, they are without offspring, because they lack good progeny and deeds worthy of esteem. In truth the offspring is not that which is on earth, but that in heaven. Therefore such men lack their inheritance, and death is their end. Although they gather wealth, they beg, for when they die they are in want, and find no rest. There is no one who pities their widows.

27.15.0.en: St. Ambrose Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare raiment as the clay [16]

27.15.1.en: The wicked heap up their wealth of silver and gold and garments, but the silver is of no use to them, but is like dust, and the garments like clay. Their treasures become a weight and burden to them, and they weigh themselves down with them.

27.15.2.en: And since silver in Holy Scripture often signifies the word of God, even when the wicked possess the Holy Scripture it becomes for them like dust, because they do not receive it to enjoy the earnest of heavenly things, but to obtain temporal blessings.

27.15.3.en: And since garments signify the righteousness of Christ, which covers the believer and keeps him from sin, if the wicked man practices some virtues for the sake of temporal glory in hypocrisy, his inner garments become filthy clay.

27.15.4.en: Until recent times many Easterners counted their costly garments together with silver and gold, as representing wealth of great value and a precious treasure. The Apostle Paul says: "I have coveted no man's silver, or gold, or apparel" (Acts 20:33). He also pointed to the value of clothing in (1 Tim 2:9): "costly array." And the Apostle James speaks of the rich: "Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten" (Jas 5:2). And when Joseph honored his brother Benjamin it was said: "he gave three hundred pieces of silver, and five changes of raiment" (Gen 45:22).

27.15.5.en: Garments were among the precious gifts that were presented as a kind of esteem, regard and honor. Samson promised to give garments to whoever solved his riddle (Judg 14:12-13, 19). And Naaman took garments with the rest of the gifts to present to the prophet Elisha (2 Kgs 5:5). And Solomon in all his glory did not refrain from accepting garments as valuable gifts (2 Chr 9:24). And Daniel was clothed with scarlet, given to him by the king to honor him (Dan 5:29).

27.15.6.en: It is told of a famous Eastern poet of the ninth century that many gifts were presented to him in his lifetime, and at his death he had 100 complete sets of clothes, 200 shirts and 500 turbans. The Hindus still give new garments at the end of the feast to every guest who attended the feast.

27.15.7.en: * Silver is usually interpreted as the purity of Holy Scripture, as it is said in another place: [The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth] (Ps 6:12). And since some long to have the word of God, not inwardly so as to be conformed to it, but outwardly to boast of it, it was said by the prophet: [All they that bear silver are cut off] (Zeph 11:1), concerning those who do not fill themselves with the word of God with inner refreshment, but clothe themselves with outward display.

27.16.0.en: He may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver [17].

27.16.1.en: "The innocent shall divide the silver," for he does not hoard it as the wicked man did who gathered it, but distributes it to the poor. [Give a portion to seven, and also to eight] (Eccl 11:2). He deposits it in a faithful treasury, which will support him on the great day of the Lord.

27.16.2.en: * "But the innocent shall divide the silver." For the innocent (who has a sincere heart) divides the silver, that is, he presents the declarations of the Lord (contained in Holy Scripture) piece by piece with discernment, and offers to each person what suits him with propriety. For the word of the Lord, which is here called silver or garments, is called in another place "spoils." The psalmist testifies to this by way of comparison, saying: [I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil] (Ps 162:119).

27.17.0.en: He buildeth his house as a moth, and as a booth that the keeper (the guard) maketh [18].

27.17.1.en: The wicked may build splendid palaces, thinking that they will give them happiness and rest, and will remain to perpetuate their memory, and they do not realize that they are like what the moth builds in an old garment, which soon vanishes completely.

27.17.2.en: * [He buildeth his house as a moth (the clothes moth)] [8]. For the moth builds itself a house by corruption.

27.17.4.en: The rich man shall lie down, but he shall not be gathered.

27.18.0.en: He openeth his eyes, and he is not [19].

27.18.1.en: When he sleeps he says: [Soul... take thine ease] (Lk 12:19). He appears to others very happy and at ease, having gathered enough for all his life and enough for his sons and grandsons. But he finds no true rest in his depths. "The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep" (Eccl 5:12).

27.18.2.en: When the wicked man closes his eyes at his death and lies down, he opens them, and finds that all he had gathered has been scattered, and supports him in nothing before the Judge.

27.18.3.en: * "When the rich man sleeps he shall take nothing with him; he openeth his eyes, and he findeth nothing" [19]. In harmony with this passage the psalmist says: [The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands] (Ps 5:76). So that the rich may find something in their hands after their death, it is said to them before death, while they hold their wealth in their hands: [Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations] (Lk 9:16).

27.18.4.en: * When the body sleeps in death, the soul awakens in true knowledge. Thus the rich man sleeps and opens his eyes, because he who dies in the body, his soul is bound to see what it feared to expect. Then it rises in true knowledge, and sees that all it had acquired is nothing, and finds itself in emptiness. It had been accustomed to exult in being filled with goods more than the rest of the world. But it sleeps and takes nothing with it. Certainly it takes nothing of the goods it had acquired. The sin of acquiring goods accompanies it, though it leaves behind everything for the sake of which it committed the sin.

27.19.0.en: Terrors take hold on him as waters, a tempest stealeth him away in the night [20].

27.19.1.en: Death becomes for the wicked man the king of terrors. He becomes like one drowning in overwhelming waters. He is terrified at his departure from this world, and is like the tempest that a whirlwind snatches away. The storm of God's wrath blows upon him "in the night," and snatches him away in the darkness he chose for himself, so that he is like one who is shaken and no one sees him to rescue him. Since he deprives himself of the rising of the Sun of Righteousness upon him, to pour out His mercy in him, he places himself under divine justice, and who can endure it?!
